challenges.title: How Large Language Models Work: Tokens and Embeddings
description: In 2026, Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, and Gemini 2.0 are the backbone of AI applications. Understanding how they work is essential for every developer.
LLMs process text as tokens — chunks of characters that are roughly 3-4 characters long on average. The word 'programming' might be split into tokens like ['pro', 'gram', 'ming'].

// Token counting approximation (like tiktoken) function estimateTokens(text) { // Rough estimate: ~4 characters per token return Math.ceil(text.length / 4); } // Common token limits (2026): // GPT-4o: 128,000 tokens context window // Claude 3.5 Sonnet: 200,000 tokens // Gemini 1.5 Pro: 1,000,000 tokens // Llama 3.1: 128,000 tokens (open source)

Embeddings are numerical representations of text (vectors of 1536+ numbers) that capture semantic meaning. Similar meanings produce similar vectors. They power semantic search, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), and recommendation systems.
Instructions

Implement a simplified cosineSimilarity function that takes two arrays (vectors) of equal length and returns their cosine similarity — a number from -1 to 1 where 1 = identical direction. This is used to find which text embeddings are most similar to a query embedding in a vector database.
challengeSeed: // Cosine similarity: the core operation in embedding search
// Used by vector DBs like Pinecone, Weaviate, pgvector
// dot product / (magnitude of A * magnitude of B)
tests: var sim = cosineSimilarity([1,0,0],[1,0,0]); assert(Math.abs(sim - 1) < 0.0001, 'message: Identical vectors should have cosine similarity of 1.');
var sim2 = cosineSimilarity([1,0],[0,1]); assert(Math.abs(sim2) < 0.0001, 'message: Perpendicular vectors should have cosine similarity of ~0.');
var sim3 = cosineSimilarity([1,2,3],[2,4,6]); assert(Math.abs(sim3 - 1) < 0.0001, 'message: Parallel vectors (same direction) should have similarity of 1.');

challenges.title: Prompt Engineering: Writing Effective AI Prompts
description: Prompt engineering is the practice of crafting inputs to AI models to get better, more reliable outputs. In 2026, it's a core skill for developers building on top of LLMs.
Key prompt techniques:

// 1. Zero-shot: Direct instruction 'Summarize this text in one sentence: [text]' // 2. Few-shot: Examples before the task 'Classify sentiment (positive/negative): Text: "I love this!" -> positive Text: "This is terrible" -> negative Text: "[your text]" ->' // 3. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) 'Solve this step by step: [problem]' // 4. System prompt: Sets model behavior { role: 'system', content: 'You are a helpful coding assistant. Always provide TypeScript examples.' } // 5. Structured output 'Return a JSON object with fields: name, age, skills[]'
Best practices for 2026: Be specific and explicit, provide context and constraints, use structured formats (JSON) for programmatic outputs, iterate and test prompts systematically.
Instructions

Write a function buildPrompt that takes a template string with placeholders like {{variable}} and a values object, and returns the template with all placeholders replaced by their corresponding values. This simulates prompt templating used in LangChain, LlamaIndex, and similar frameworks.
challengeSeed: // Prompt templating - used in LangChain, PromptLayer, etc.
// '{{name}} is {{age}} years old' + {name: 'Alice', age: 30} -> 'Alice is 30 years old'
tests: assert(buildPrompt('Hello, {{name}}!', {name: 'Alice'}) === 'Hello, Alice!', 'message: Should replace {{name}} with Alice.');
assert(buildPrompt('{{a}} + {{b}} = {{c}}', {a: 1, b: 2, c: 3}) === '1 + 2 = 3', 'message: Should replace multiple placeholders.');
assert(buildPrompt('Hi {{name}}, you are {{age}}.', {name: 'Bob', age: 25}) === 'Hi Bob, you are 25.', 'message: Should work with number values.');
assert(buildPrompt('{{missing}} value', {}) === '{{missing}} value', 'message: Should leave unresolved placeholders intact.');

challenges.title: RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
description: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is the dominant architecture for AI apps in 2026. Instead of relying solely on a model's training data, RAG retrieves relevant documents from your own data store and injects them into the prompt.

// RAG Pipeline (conceptual) async function ragQuery(userQuestion: string): Promise<string> { // 1. Embed the user's question const queryEmbedding = await embedText(userQuestion); // 2. Find the most similar chunks in your vector DB const relevantChunks = await vectorDB.search(queryEmbedding, topK=5); // 3. Build a context-rich prompt const context = relevantChunks.map(c => c.text).join('\n---\n'); const prompt = `Answer based on context:\n${context}\nQuestion: ${userQuestion}`; // 4. Generate answer with LLM return await llm.complete(prompt); }

RAG is used for: company knowledge bases, document Q&A, code search, customer support bots, and medical reference systems. The key challenge is chunking strategy — how to split documents into meaningful pieces.
Instructions

Write a function chunkText that splits a long text string into overlapping chunks for RAG indexing. It should take text, chunkSize (max characters per chunk), and overlap (characters shared between adjacent chunks). Return an array of chunk strings.
challengeSeed: // Used before embedding text into a vector database
// Create chunks from position 0, step, 2*step, etc.
// Each chunk is text.slice(start, start + chunkSize)
tests: var chunks = chunkText('abcdefghij', 4, 0); assert(chunks.length >= 2 && chunks[0] === 'abcd', 'message: First chunk should be \'abcd\' with no overlap.');
var c2 = chunkText('abcdefghij', 4, 2); assert(c2[0] === 'abcd' && c2[1] === 'cdef', 'message: With overlap=2, second chunk should start 2 chars into first chunk.');
var c3 = chunkText('hello', 10, 0); assert(c3.length === 1 && c3[0] === 'hello', 'message: Text shorter than chunkSize should produce one chunk.');

challenges.title: AI Agent Patterns: Tools and Function Calling
description: AI Agents are LLM-powered programs that can use tools — web search, code execution, APIs, database queries — to complete complex multi-step tasks. In 2026, agent frameworks like LangGraph, AutoGen, and CrewAI are standard in production.

// OpenAI Function Calling format (used by all major LLMs) const tools = [ { type: 'function', function: { name: 'get_weather', description: 'Get current weather for a city', parameters: { type: 'object', properties: { city: { type: 'string', description: 'City name' }, units: { type: 'string', enum: ['celsius', 'fahrenheit'] } }, required: ['city'] } } } ]; // The model decides WHEN to call the tool and WITH WHAT arguments // Your code then executes it and feeds results back to the model
The agent loop: LLM receives task → decides to call a tool → your code runs the tool → results fed back to LLM → LLM continues reasoning → repeat until task complete.
Instructions
Implement a simple ToolRegistry that stores tools (name → function mapping) and a dispatch method that looks up and calls a tool by name with given arguments. Return null if the tool doesn't exist.
challengeSeed: // Simulates the tool dispatcher in an AI agent framework
// Look up tool by name, call with args, return result
// Return null if tool not found
// Return array of registered tool names
tests: var registry = createToolRegistry(); registry.register('add', function(a) { return a.x + a.y; }); assert(registry.dispatch('add', {x: 3, y: 4}) === 7, 'message: dispatch should call registered tool with args.');
assert(registry.dispatch('nonexistent', {}) === null, 'message: dispatch should return null for unknown tools.');
registry.register('greet', function(a) { return 'Hello ' + a.name; }); assert(registry.list().length === 2, 'message: list() should return all registered tool names.');
